paragraphs: “Your nerves are shot,” remarked the gentleman, in an easy, careless manner that was still perfectly polite. “You’re angry with me even for catching cold, though it happened in the most natural way. I was in a hurry that day. I was on my way to a diplomatic _soirée_ at the house of a high-ranking lady in Petersburg, who was angling for influence in the Ministry. So there I was in evening dress, white tie and gloves, and yet I was God knows where, and I had to fly through space to get to your earth.... It took only an instant, of course. But a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes, and just picture it, in an evening suit and open waistcoat. Spirits don’t freeze, but when one’s in the flesh, well ... in short, I didn’t stop to think. I simply set off. And you know, up in those ethereal spaces, in the water above the firmament, the frost is such that ... well, you can’t even call it frost. Imagine, 150 degrees below zero! You know the game the village girls play? They invite some unsuspecting fellow to lick an ax when it’s thirty degrees below. His tongue freezes to it on the spot, and the poor dupe tears off the skin and bleeds. But that’s only at 30 degrees. At 150, I imagine, you’d just have to touch the ax with your finger and that would be the end of you ... if only there could be an ax there.”
“And can there be an ax there?” Ivan cut in, with careless contempt. He was straining with all his might not to believe in the delusion, and not to slip into complete madness.
“An ax?” the guest broke in, surprised.
“Yes! What would become of an ax up there?” Ivan cried suddenly, with a savage, dogged stubbornness.

“What would become of an ax in space? _Quelle idée!_ If it dropped some distance, I think it would simply start circling the earth, not knowing why, like a satellite. The astronomers would work out when the ax rises and sets, _Gatzuk_ would put it in his almanac, and that’s all.”

“You’re stupid, awfully stupid,” said Ivan peevishly. “Tell cleverer lies or I won’t listen. You’re trying to beat me with realism, to prove to me that you exist. But I don’t want to believe you exist! I won’t believe it!”

“But I’m not lying. Every word is true. Unfortunately the truth is hardly ever amusing. I see you keep expecting something big from me, and perhaps something fine. What a pity. I only give what I can—”
“Don’t talk philosophy, you ass!”

“Philosophy, he says, when my whole right side is numb and I’m moaning and groaning! I’ve been through the entire medical faculty. They diagnose beautifully, they have your whole disease at their fingertips, but they haven’t the slightest idea how to cure you. I met an enthusiastic young student here. ‘You may die,’ he told me, ‘but you’ll know exactly what disease you’re dying of!’ And then there’s their way of packing people off to specialists! ‘We only diagnose,’ they say, ‘but go and see so-and-so, he’ll cure you.’ The old doctor who treated every kind of illness has vanished altogether, I assure you. Nowadays there are only specialists, and every one of them advertises in the papers. Trouble with your nose? They send you to Paris, where, they say, a European specialist cures noses. In Paris he examines your nose and says: I can cure only your right nostril. I don’t treat the left one, that’s not my specialty. Go to Vienna, there’s a man there who will cure your left nostril. What are you supposed to do? I fell back on folk remedies. A German doctor told me to rub myself with honey and salt in the bathhouse. I went just to get an extra bath, smeared myself from head to foot, and it did me no good whatever. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. Bless him, he sent me a book and some drops, and, can you believe it, Hoff’s malt extract cured me! I bought it by accident, drank a bottle and a half, and I was ready to dance. The whole thing vanished. I resolved to write to the newspapers and thank him, moved by gratitude. And can you believe it, that caused no end of trouble. Not one paper would take my letter. ‘It would be very reactionary,’ they said, ‘nobody will believe it. _Le diable n’existe point._ Better stay anonymous,’ they advised. What good is a thank-you letter if it’s anonymous? I joked with the men at the newspaper office. ‘These days it’s reactionary to believe in God,’ I said, ‘but I’m the devil, so people may believe in me.’ ‘We quite understand,’ they said. ‘Who doesn’t believe in the devil? Even so, it won’t do, it could hurt our reputation. As a joke, if you like.’ But I thought, as a joke it wouldn’t be very witty. So it never got printed. And would you believe it, I’m sore about it to this day. My finest feelings, gratitude for one, are literally closed to me, just because of my position in society.”
“Philosophical reflections again?” Ivan snarled with spite.

“Heaven forbid. But a man can’t help complaining now and then. I’m a slandered man. Every minute you reproach me for being stupid. One can tell you’re young. My dear fellow, brains aren’t everything! I have a kind and merry heart by nature. ‘I also write vaudevilles of all sorts.’ You seem to take me for Hlestakov grown old, but my fate is a far more serious one. Before time began, by some decree I could never make sense of, I was fated ‘to deny.’ Yet I’m genuinely good-hearted, and not in the least inclined to negation. ‘No, you must go and deny. Without denial there’s no criticism, and what would a journal be without its column of criticism?’ Without criticism it would be one long ‘hosannah.’ But nothing but hosannah won’t do for life. The hosannah has to be tested in the crucible of doubt, and so on, in the same vein. I don’t meddle in all that, though. I didn’t create it, and I’m not answerable for it. Well, they chose their scapegoat. They made me write the column of criticism, and so life became possible. We understand that comedy. I, for instance, simply ask to be annihilated. No, they tell me, live, because without you there would be nothing. If everything in the universe were reasonable, nothing would ever happen. There would be no events without you, and events there must be. So I serve, against the grain, to bring events about, and I do what’s irrational because I’m ordered to. For all their undoubted intelligence, men take this farce seriously, and that is their tragedy. They suffer, of course ... but then they live. They live a real life, not an imaginary one, because suffering is life. Without suffering, where would the pleasure be? Everything would turn into one endless church service: holy, but dull. And what about me? I suffer, and still I don’t live. I’m the x in an indeterminate equation. I’m a kind of phantom in life, who has lost every beginning and every end, and has even forgotten his own name. You’re laughing—no, you’re not laughing, you’re angry again. You’re always angry. All you care about is intelligence. But I tell you again, I would give up this whole super-stellar life, all the ranks and honors, just to be turned into the soul of a merchant’s wife weighing eighteen stone and to light candles at God’s shrine.”
“So even you don’t believe in God?” said Ivan, with a smile full of hatred.
“What can I say?—that is, if you’re serious—”
“Is there a God or not?” Ivan cried, with the same savage intensity.
“Ah, so you are serious! My dear fellow, I swear I don’t know. There! I’ve said it!”
“You don’t know, but you see God? No, you’re not someone apart. You’re me, you’re I and nothing more! You’re rubbish, you’re something I’ve dreamed up!”

“Well, if you like, my philosophy is the same as yours, and that would be right. _Je pense, donc je suis_. That much I know for a fact. All the rest, all these worlds, God, even Satan, none of it is proved, as far as I can see. Does it exist on its own, or is it only an emanation of me, a logical development of my ego, which alone has existed forever? But I’d better stop at once, because I suspect you’re about to jump up and beat me.”
“You’d better tell me some anecdote!” said Ivan miserably.

“There’s an anecdote exactly on our subject. Or rather a legend, not an anecdote. You see, you reproach me with unbelief: you say, you see me, yet you don’t believe. But, my dear fellow, I’m not the only one. We’re all in a muddle up there now, and all because of your science. We used to have atoms, five senses, four elements, and somehow everything hung together. There were atoms even in the ancient world. But once we learned that you had discovered the chemical molecule and protoplasm and the devil knows what, we had to lower our crest. It’s a real muddle, and above all there’s superstition and scandal. We have as much scandal among us as you have among you, you know, a little more in fact. And spying, too, since we have our own secret police department that receives private information. Well, this wild legend belongs to our Middle Ages—not yours, ours—and nobody believes it, even among us, except the old ladies of eighteen stone. Not your old ladies, I mean ours. We have everything you have. I’m giving away one of our secrets out of friendship for you, though it’s forbidden. The legend is about Paradise. They say there was once a thinker and philosopher here on earth. He rejected everything: ‘laws, conscience, faith,’ and above all the life to come. He died expecting to go straight into darkness and death, and found a future life in front of him. He was astounded and indignant. ‘This is against my principles!’ he said. And for that he was punished ... that is, you must forgive me, I’m only repeating what I heard myself, it’s only a legend ... he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in the dark (we’ve gone metric, you know). When he has finished that quadrillion, the gates of heaven will be opened to him and he’ll be forgiven—”
“And what tortures do you have in the other world, apart from the quadrillion kilometers?” asked Ivan, with a strange eagerness.

“Tortures? Ah, don’t ask. In the old days we had all kinds, but now they’ve gone in mostly for moral punishments—‘the stings of conscience’ and all that nonsense. We picked that up from you, too, from the softening of your manners. And who is better off for it? Only those with no conscience, since how can conscience torture people who haven’t got one? But decent people who do have a conscience and a sense of honor suffer for it. Reforms do nothing but harm when the ground hasn’t been prepared for them, especially institutions copied from abroad! The old fire was better. Well, this man who was condemned to the quadrillion kilometers stood still, looked around, and lay down across the road. ‘I won’t go. I refuse on principle!’ Take the soul of an enlightened Russian atheist, mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked three days and nights in the belly of the whale, and you have the character of that thinker lying across the road.”
“What did he lie on there?”
“Well, I suppose there was something to lie on. You’re not laughing?”
“Bravo!” cried Ivan, with the same strange eagerness. Now he was listening with unexpected curiosity. “Well, is he lying there still?”
“That’s just it, he isn’t. He lay there nearly a thousand years, and then he got up and went on.”

“What an ass!” cried Ivan, laughing nervously, but still seeming to ponder something intently. “Does it make any difference whether he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take a billion years to walk it, wouldn’t it?”
“A good deal more than that. I haven’t a pencil and paper or I’d work it out. But he got there long ago, and that’s where the story really starts.”
“What, he got there? But where did he find a billion years to do it?”

“You keep thinking of our present earth! But our present earth may have been repeated a billion times. It dies out, freezes, cracks, breaks into pieces, falls apart into its elements, becomes again ‘the water above the firmament,’ then a comet again, a sun again, and from the sun it turns into earth again. And that same sequence may have been repeated without end, exactly the same down to the last detail, most unseemly and unbearably tedious—”
“Well, well, what happened when he got there?”

“Well, the moment the gates of Paradise opened and he stepped inside, before he’d been there two seconds by his watch (though I think his watch must have dissolved into its elements long before, on the way), he cried out that those two seconds were worth walking not a quadrillion kilometers but a quadrillion of quadrillions, raised to the quadrillionth power! In short, he sang ‘hosannah’ and overdid it so badly that certain persons of lofty ideas there wouldn’t even shake hands with him at first. He’d turned reactionary too fast, they said. The Russian temperament. I repeat, it’s a legend. I give it for what it’s worth. So that’s the kind of ideas we still have about such matters.”

“I’ve caught you!” Ivan cried, with almost childish delight, as if he had at last remembered something. “That anecdote about the quadrillion years, I made it up myself! I was seventeen, still at the high school. I made up that anecdote and told it to a schoolmate named Korovkin, in Moscow.... The anecdote is so typical of me that I couldn’t have taken it from anywhere. I thought I’d forgotten it ... but I recalled it without knowing—I recalled it myself—it wasn’t you telling it! Thousands of things come back unconsciously like that, even to people being led to execution ... it’s come back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You’re a dream, not a living creature!”
“The violence with which you deny my existence,” the gentleman laughed, “convinces me that you do believe in me.”
“Not in the least! I haven’t a hundredth part of a grain of faith in you!”
“But you have a thousandth of a grain. Homeopathic doses, perhaps, are the strongest. Admit that you have faith down to the ten-thousandth of a grain.”
“Not for a minute,” cried Ivan furiously. “But I’d like to believe in you,” he added, oddly.

“Aha! An admission! But I’m good-natured, so I’ll help you out again. Listen, I was the one who caught you, not you me. I told you your own anecdote, which you’d forgotten, on purpose, to destroy your faith in me altogether.”
“You’re lying. You came here to convince me that you exist!”
